items.title: Sampling strategy affects every fieldwork result
items.claim: Why does a geographer choose a stratified sample over a random one?

options.text: Stratified sampling deliberately includes proportions from defined subgroups (e.g. age categories in a questionnaire, river sections by gradient), reducing risk of missing minority categories

items.reveal:
Sampling types: random (every member equally likely), systematic (every nth member, e.g. every 10 metres along a transect), stratified (proportional samples from defined groups), opportunistic (whoever is available — least rigorous).

At A-level, the NEA Independent Investigation requires explicit justification of sampling strategy. Small samples (n<30) limit statistical analysis; sub-group analysis needs larger samples in each stratum.

Fieldwork ethics, including consent for questionnaires and impact on study sites, has become more prominent.
items.why: Bad sampling produces bad results regardless of how impressive the spreadsheet looks. Sampling design is upstream of all subsequent analysis.

items.title: Stratified sampling deliberately includes defined subgroups
items.claim: Why use stratified sampling rather than random?

options.text: Stratified sampling deliberately includes proportions from defined subgroups (e.g. age categories in a questionnaire, river sections by gradient), reducing the risk of missing minority categories

items.reveal:
Sampling types: random (every member equally likely), systematic (every nth member — e.g. every 10 m along a river transect), stratified (proportional samples from defined groups), opportunistic (whoever is available — least rigorous).

GCSE and A-level NEA fieldwork requires explicit justification of sampling strategy. Small samples (n<30) limit statistical analysis; subgroup analysis needs larger samples in each stratum.

Fieldwork ethics — informed consent for questionnaires, minimising impact on study sites — has become more prominent in awarding-body specifications.
items.why: Bad sampling produces bad results regardless of subsequent analysis. Sampling design is upstream of every statistical inference — and is the most common point of failure in student fieldwork.

items.title: Most of Britain was under ice 20,000 years ago
items.claim: How much of the UK was covered by ice at the Last Glacial Maximum?

options.text: None — Britain has never been glaciated
Most of the country north of the Thames was under ice up to around 1 km thick at the LGM (around 20,000 years ago), with southern England as a permafrost tundra zone
Only the Scottish Highlands were glaciated
All of the UK was under permanent ice until 1500 CE

items.reveal:
The British-Irish Ice Sheet extended to roughly the Thames-Severn line. Ice was up to 1 km thick over the Highlands. Glacial landforms — corries (Snowdonia, Lake District), U-shaped valleys (Glencoe), drumlins (Eden Valley) and erratics (Norber, Yorkshire) — record the maximum.

The Younger Dryas (around 12,900-11,700 years ago) was a final cold snap with small Highland glaciers (the Loch Lomond Stadial). Britain became ice-free by around 10,000 years ago.

Britain rejoined Europe geographically about 8,200 years ago when the Storegga submarine landslide tsunami finished off Doggerland.
items.why: Most British landforms are products of the Ice Ages, not earlier processes. The shape of the country is recent and contingent.
